title: Taurine supplementation and systemic lupus erythematosus in preclinical studies: a systematic review of clinical outcomes and underlying mechanisms

sections.abstract: Taurine (Tau) is a sulfur-containing amino acid that has therapeutic roles in several diseases, including inflammatory conditions. The involvement of Tau in modulating systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) autoimmunity has been indicated in preclinical models, but reports are contradictory. This systematic review aimed to summarize current research regarding the potential role of Tau in SLE, to notice knowledge gaps, and to offer suggestions for the way ahead. The literature search was carried out using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar databases until October 2025. Search alert services were also applied to notice related papers published after the primary search. All studies investigating the effects of Tau in SLE that met the inclusion criteria were eligible. Out of 77 articles initially found, only six preclinical studies (animal and in-vitro) were eligible, and no qualified clinical study was identified. Five studies indicated that Tau was helpful in improving clinical parameters, decreasing T helper 1 (Th1) and Th17 cells and inflammatory mediators (e.g., tumor necrosis factor-α, C-reactive protein, and inducible nitric oxide synthase), removing reactive oxygen species and decreasing oxidative markers like malondialdehyde, increasing regulatory T (Treg) and Th2 cells and anti-inflammatory interleukin-4 and interleukin-10 cytokines, increasing antioxidant enzymes superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase, and inhibiting both FAS- and mitochondrial-dependent apoptotic signaling components. However, only one preclinical study reported that Tau aggravated SLE progression characterized by increased generation of type I interferons, enhanced autoantibodies and proteinuria, further lymphocyte activation, and critical nephritis. The current review provides evidence about the role of Tau in SLE and highlights the importance of further well-designed clinical trials to confirm these results, establish optimal dose and assess safety and long-term efficacy.
sections.introduction:
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease that affects multiple systems in the body, characterized by a relapsing and remitting progression. It is more common in women of childbearing age than in men (Ameer et al. 2022 ). This disease contributes to a high economic burden on patients and communities. The precise etiology of SLE is not fully understood and it is considered a multifactorial disease. It has been shown that environmental and genetic factors interact to elicit immunological responses, resulting in the overproduction of pathogenic autoantibodies and cytokine dysregulation, which lead to various clinical manifestations as well as tissue and organ damage (Ameer et al. 2022 ).

Treatment of the disease is challenging due to the unpredictable course and the involvement of numerous organs. SLE treatment is primarily based on achieving reduced disease activity or, preferably, remission (Katarzyna et al. 2023 ). Glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, and biologics are diverse medications proposed as therapeutic options (Katarzyna et al. 2023 ). However, due to the short-term adverse effects, serious long-term complications, and higher costs (Figueroa-Parra et al. 2024 ; Bultink et al. 2021 ), the use of adjuvant therapies particularly nutritional agents, has received incremental attention.

Taurine (Tau) is a sulfur-containing amino acid that is provided both exogenously from the diet and endogenously from cysteine and methionine. It is present in different mammalian tissues and plays a significant role in biological processes such as bile salt synthesis, osmoregulation, cell membrane stabilization, detoxification, cell proliferation, calcium homeostasis, central nervous system modulation, and immunomodulation, as well as anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-apoptotic activities. Tau is a semi-essential amino acid; however, it is essential in some situations related to enhanced inflammation and oxidative stress (Malek Mahdavi and Javadivala 2021 ). Recent studies have clarified therapeutic the roles of Tau in several diseases, including cardiovascular diseases, neurological disorders, mitochondrial diseases, metabolic problems (e.g., diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome), and inflammatory conditions such as arthritis (Schaffer 2018 ).

The involvement of Tau in modulating SLE autoimmunity has been indicated in preclinical models (Huang et al. 2009 , 2025 ; Luo et al. 2021 ; Li et al. 2020 ; Hsu et al. 2008 , 2010 ), but reports are contradictory. To the best of our knowledge, no systematic review has yet incorporated these data to augment our understanding. Therefore, to fill the present knowledge gap, we designed the current systematic review to collect and review the available evidence regarding Tau and SLE.
sections.methods:
The study protocol has been registered on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) website (CRD420251172479). The present systematic review adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) checklist (Moher et al. 2015 ). Figure 1 provides the PRISMA flowchart of study search and selection.

Fig. 1 PRISMA (preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses) flowchart of study search and selection

PRISMA (preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses) flowchart of study search and selection

We performed a search of the following electronic databases up to October 2025: PubMed, Scopus, ISI Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The search terms used included both MESH and non-MESH terms such as (Taurine OR Taufon OR Tauphon OR “Taurine, Monopotassium Salt” OR “Taurine Zinc Salt (2:1)” OR “Taurine Hydrochloride”) AND (“Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic” OR “Lupus Erythematosus Disseminatus” OR “Systemic Lupus Erythematosus” OR “Libman-Sacks Disease” OR “Disease, Libman-Sacks” OR “Libman Sacks Disease”). There were no restrictions on language or publication date. Two authors (Aida Malek Mahdavi and Niloufar Orooji) independently conducted searches, screened articles, and extracted data. Redundant studies were removed, and any discrepancies were resolved by the third author (Zeinab Javadivala). References in selected publications were also examined for additional relevant studies.

Studies with these characteristics were included: (a) evaluating the effect of Tau on clinical or biochemical parameters related to SLE in comparison with the control group; (b) having an accessible full-text. Studies with these characteristics were excluded: (a) review articles; (b) book chapters; (c) patents, theses, and congress abstracts; (d) combination studies (publications examining the effects of Tau in combination with other compounds on SLE, which might obscure Tau-specific effects); (e) studies examining the effects of Tau in other disorders. Based on the specified search terms and inclusion criteria, six papers remained.

Two independent reviewers (Aida Malek Mahdavi and Niloufar Orooji) extracted data from the relevant studies. The information obtained from the articles included the first author’s name, publication time, population characteristics, form and dosage of intervention, treatment duration, and outcomes. Any potential conflicts were resolved by the third reviewer (Zeinab Javadivala). A summary of the reviewed studies is presented in Tables 1 and 2 .

All relevant studies were evaluated for potential bias risk using the Checklist for Reporting In-vitro Studies (CRIS) guideline for in-vitro research and SYRCLE’s risk of bias tool for animal research (Malek Mahdavi and Javadivala 2021 ). The SYRCLE risk of bias analysis had six domains, and each domain was assessed as having a high, unclear, or low risk of bias.
sections.results:
The risk of bias was evaluated across all six included studies (Fig. 2 ). An unclear risk of bias was identified in several domains: selection bias (due to missing data on randomization procedures; n = 5), performance bias (researchers not blinded to intervention types; n = 6), and baseline characteristics for animal studies ( n = 3). Attrition bias was low in all six studies, while reporting bias was present in all six studies. Additionally, detection bias was high due to a lack of blinding in outcome assessment ( n = 2).

Fig. 2 Risk of bias assessment of studies ( n = 6)

Risk of bias assessment of studies ( n = 6)

We initially found 77 papers (Fig. 1 ). After removing duplicates, 45 studies were screened based on titles and abstracts. Subsequently, 39 review or irrelevant papers were excluded, leaving six papers for further analysis. Among these, four studies focused solely on animal models, whereas two studies included both animal and in-vitro models. No relevant clinical research was found among the selected papers. Tables 1 and 2 provide detailed information on the investigations.

Table 1 presents animal studies included in the current systematic review.

The effects of Tau on clinical and histologic parameters were examined in all animal studies. Tau decreased spleen index and renal lesions in SLE mice (Huang et al. 2025 ) and improved histopathological changes such as mesangial matrix dilation and glomerular hypertrophy in lupus nephritis (LN) mice (Luo et al. 2021 ) compared with disease control groups. Furthermore, Hsu et al. ( 2010 ) showed that Tau (10 g/kg diet, oral for 12 weeks) decreased lipid deposition in liver tissues in NZB/W F1 mice (as an SLE animal model) fed with a high-cholesterol diet compared to the high-cholesterol-fed diet control group. Also, Tau (1% in the diet, oral for 12 weeks) led to a reduction in ventricular myocardium abnormal architecture and TUNEL-positive cells in the left ventricles of hearts (Huang et al. 2009 ) as well as a decreased percentage of TUNEL-positive hepatic cells in the liver (Hsu et al. 2008 ) in NZB/W F1 mice fed with a high-cholesterol diet compared to the high-cholesterol diet-fed control group. In addition, Huang et al. ( 2009 ) reported that Tau reduced cardiac fibrosis, collagen deposition, and myofibril disarray in NZB/W F1 mice fed with a high-cholesterol diet compared to the high-cholesterol diet-fed control group. In contrast, Li et al. ( 2020 ) demonstrated that Tau (1% in drinking water oral for 10 weeks) aggravated SLE progression. Compared with the SLE control group, Tau-treated SLE mice showed splenomegaly, increased circulating levels of autoantibodies and mean glomerular size, proteinuria, cellular infiltrations, severe glomerular lesions, and enhanced expression of numerous interferon (IFN)-α/β target genes in the kidney (Li et al. 2020 ).

The effects of Tau on different metabolic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, immune, and apoptosis parameters were examined in all animal studies. Tau decreased serum immunoglobulin G (IgG) and anti-double stranded-DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibody levels, proteinuria, urine blood urea nitrogen (BUN), complement component 3 (C3) and IgG deposition in glomeruli, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels in the kidneys of SLE mice (Huang et al. 2025 ). It also led to a reduction in serum creatinine, BUN, proteinuria, and renal tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), malondialdehyde (MDA), and ROS levels, while enhancing superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione peroxidase (GPx), interleukin (IL)-4, and IL-10 levels in LN mice (Luo et al. 2021 ) compared with disease control groups. In a study on NZB/W F1 mice fed a high-cholesterol diet, Hsu et al. ( 2010 ) showed that Tau decreased serum triglyceride, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels as well as C-reactive protein (CRP) levels in liver lysate compared to the high-cholesterol-fed diet control group. Additionally, Tau decreased the levels of heat shock proteins (HSPs) 70 and 90, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP), and iNOS in liver lysate compared to the high-cholesterol-fed diet control group (Hsu et al. 2010 ). Furthermore, Tau decreased T helper 1 (Th1) and T helper 17 (Th17) cells and increased regulatory T (Treg) and T helper 2 (Th2) cell proportion in the spleen compared with the SLE control group (Huang et al. 2025 ). However, no significant changes occurred in the T follicular helper (Tfh) cell proportion compared with the SLE control mice (Huang et al. 2025 ). Reduction in kidney tissue apoptosis and inactivation of the nuclear factor (NF)-κB p65 signaling pathway were also demonstrated in Tau-treated LN mice compared with the LN control group (Luo et al. 2021 ). In another study on NZB/W F1 mice fed a high-cholesterol diet, Huang et al. ( 2009 ) reported that Tau reduced TNF-α, TNF receptor superfamily member 6 (FAS) ligands and receptors, and FAS-associated death domain (FADD) as well as apoptotic executors (e.g., activated caspase-8, truncated form of BH3-interacting domain death agonist (tBid), apoptosis regulator Bax (Bax), activated caspase-9, and caspase-3) in left ventricles of hearts compared with the high-cholesterol diet-fed control group. Moreover, Tau decreased fibroblast growth factor (FGF), phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (p-ERK), urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA), MMP-2, and MMP-9 levels in the left ventricles of hearts, whereas it increased B-cell lymphoma-2 (Bcl-2), insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R), and phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3K) protein levels as well as phosphorylated serine/threonine protein kinase (p-AKT)/AKT ratio in left ventricles of hearts compared with the high-cholesterol diet-fed control group (Huang et al. 2009 ). Hsu et al. ( 2008 ) also suggested that Tau reduced hepatic apoptosis, as demonstrated by lower caspase-3 activity and diminished DNA nicking in the liver of NZB/W F1 mice fed a high-cholesterol diet compared to the high-cholesterol diet-fed control group. Additionally, Tau reduced the expression of important proteins associated with apoptosis (e.g., FAS, caspase-8, active caspase-9, and apoptotic protease activating factor 1 (Apaf-1), Bax, Bcl-2 associated agonist of cell death (BAD), cytochrome c, and phosphorylated P38 proteins in liver compared with high-cholesterol diet-fed control mice (Hsu et al. 2008 ). However, increased liver levels of Bcl-2 and activated ERK-1/2 through phosphorylation, as well as enhanced levels of phosphorylated AKT and NF-κB (p65) proteins in the liver were reported in Tau-treated mice fed a high-cholesterol diet compared with the high-cholesterol diet-fed control group (Hsu et al. 2008 ). In contrast, Li et al. ( 2020 ) showed that Tau augmented the proportion and activation of plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), total B and T cells, activated CD4 + , CD8 + , and CD44 + T cells, the percentage of IL17A + and IFNγ + CD4 + T cells, and IFNγ + CD8 + T cells in SLE mice compared with the SLE control group. Additionally, the population of age-associated B cells (ABCs), the CD19 + CD23 − CD21 − AA4.1 − splenic ABC population, and the levels of TNFα and IL-6 cytokines were enhanced in Tau-treated mice compared with the SLE control group. Loss of the marginal zone B cell population and the CD23 – CD21 high marginal zone B cell compartment was also reported compared with the SLE control group.

Table 2 presents in-vitro studies included in the current systematic review. According to Huang et al. ( 2025 ), Tau (2, 20, and 50mM) reduced the percentage of Th17 cells and increased the percentage of Treg cells dose-dependently in PBMCs of SLE patients. Furthermore, in splenocytes from Resiquimod (R848)-induced SLE mice, treatment with 20 mM Tau reduced abnormal oxidation, proliferation, and senescence of CD4 + T cells, percentages of ROS, Ki-67, SPiDER-βGal, P21, and Treg in CD4 + T cells, and p-S6 in CD8 + T cells (Huang et al. 2025 ). However, no changes were reported in CD4 + T cell activation and apoptosis as well as p-AKT in CD8 + T cells (Huang et al. 2025 ). In another study on human primary pDCs separated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of SLE patients and mouse primary pDCs isolated from the spleen of C57BL/6J mice, Li et al. ( 2020 ) demonstrated that treatment with 20 mM Tau decreased the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP)/NADPH ratio, ROS level, and neutrophil cytosolic factor-1 (NCF1) expression. Moreover, Tau increased IFN-α, IFN-β, and TNF-α levels, as well as increased expression of major histocompatibility complex II (Li et al. 2020 ). In addition, Tau enhanced the phosphorylation level and activation of interferon regulatory factor-7 (IRF7) and S6K and led to an increased PI3K-mTOR signal (Li et al. 2020 ). However, there was no change in the expression of co-stimulatory molecule CD86 (Li et al. 2020 ).
sections.discussion:
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic review of Tau’s effects on SLE according to the currently available research. Most studies indicated that Tau was helpful in improving clinical and histological parameters, alleviating inflammation and oxidative stress, and modulating immunologic responses in SLE (Huang et al. 2009 , 2025 ; Luo et al. 2021 ; Hsu et al. 2008 , 2010 ). However, only one study indicated that Tau aggravated SLE progression, which was characterized by increased generation of type I IFNs, higher IFN-induced gene expression, enhanced autoantibodies and proteinuria, further lymphocyte activation, and critical nephritis (Li et al. 2020 ). This discrepancy may be due to differences in study animals and/or cell types, study environment, metabolic modulation of immune responses, dosage, and duration of the intervention.

SLE is a chronic autoimmune disorder, and its pathogenesis is linked to the dysregulation of various immune cells, particularly CD4 + T cells, DCs, and macrophages, causing systemic inflammation and organ damage (Ameer et al. 2022 ). Inflammation has a close relationship with oxidative stress, which also plays a vital role in the pathophysiology and complications of SLE. Oxidative stress leads to an imbalance between Th17 and Treg cells in SLE, characterized by enhanced proinflammatory Th17 cells and decreased anti-inflammatory Treg cells as well as aggravated autoimmune injury (Yang et al. 2016 ). Oxidative stress also causes an abnormal increase in apoptosis and a delay in the clearance of apoptotic bodies. This delay in apoptotic cell clearance contributes to the interaction between ROS and nuclear residues and the generation of neo-epitopes that subsequently stimulate autoantibody generation, leading to inflammation and organ damage in SLE (Shah et al. 2014 ).

It has been indicated that Tau, through various anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-apoptotic mechanisms, can be helpful in managing SLE. Tau can decrease inflammatory Th1 and Th17 cells and increase anti-inflammatory Treg cells and Th2 cells (Huang et al. 2025 ). In addition, Tau can decrease abnormal oxidation, proliferation, and senescence of CD4 + T cells (Huang et al. 2025 ). Also, Tau, by reducing inflammatory parameters (e.g., TNF-α, CRP, HSP70, HSP90, and iNOS) and enhancing anti-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-4 and IL-10), can play a role in SLE management (Luo et al. 2021 ; Hsu et al. 2010 ). In addition, Tau, via reducing fibrosis and fibrotic signaling components like FGF, p-ERK, ERK, uPA, MMP-2, and MMP-9, exhibits cardiac protective features in SLE (Huang et al. 2009 ). Enhanced levels of IGF1R and related downstream signaling components including, PI3K and P-Akt, in the heart also suggest the role of Tau in cardiac survival in SLE (Huang et al. 2009 ). The antioxidant effect of Tau can be mediated through removing ROS, decreasing oxidative markers (e.g., MDA), and enhancing antioxidant enzymes (e.g., SOD and GPx) (Huang et al. 2025 ; Luo et al. 2021 ), which is also helpful in SLE management. The principal source of ROS in cells is mitochondria, which are neutralized by SOD, GPX, and catalase enzymes following mitochondrial leakage (Vakifahmetoglu-Norberg et al. 2017 ; Ighodaro and Akinloye 2018 ). Tau interferes with the cellular effects of ROS by enhancing the function of the above-mentioned antioxidant enzymes (Luo et al. 2021 ). Furthermore, Tau exerts anti-apoptotic effects in different tissues, including the kidney, heart, and liver, by inhibiting both FAS- and mitochondrial-dependent apoptotic signaling components such as TNF-α, FAS ligand, FAS receptors, FADD, activated caspase-8, t-Bid, Bad, Bax, activated caspase-9, activated caspase-3, cytochrome c, Apaf-1, and apoptotic-positive cells (Luo et al. 2021 ; Huang et al. 2009 ; Hsu et al. 2008 ). Caspases are indispensable parts of the apoptotic pathway. Caspase-3 is assumed to be the main caspase and can be activated by initiator caspases (e.g., caspase-8, caspase-9, or caspase-10). Caspase-3 particularly induces the endonuclease caspase-activated DNase (CAD). In proliferating cells, CAD binds to the inhibitor of CAD (ICAD). In apoptotic cells, activated caspase-3 separates ICAD to make CAD free (Sakahira et al. 1998 ). Moreover, Tau, by increasing the phosphorylation of Akt, ERK1/2, and NF-κB proteins as well as decreasing the phosphorylation of the p38 protein (also known as a mediator of apoptotic cell death), promotes cell survival, indicating the involvement of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) survival signaling pathway and p38-mediated apoptotic pathway in Tau-induced anti-hepatic apoptosis (Hsu et al. 2008 ). Tau can block inflammation, oxidative stress, and tissue apoptosis by suppressing the NF-κB p65 pathway, thereby improving LN (Luo et al. 2021 ). Tau deactivates the NF-κB signaling pathway by suppressing p65 phosphorylation (Luo et al. 2021 ). Similarly, Meyer-Schwesinger et al. ( 2009 ) suggested the reduction of NF-κB p65 improved renal failure in a Rho kinase inhibition mouse model. Figure 3 presents the possible mechanisms of the effects of Tau in SLE.

Fig. 3 Schematic illustration of the mechanisms by which taurine affects systemic lupus erythematosus

Schematic illustration of the mechanisms by which taurine affects systemic lupus erythematosus

The current study had some limitations. First, lack of clinical trials assessing the effects of Tau in SLE is a significant drawback, and additional research should be conducted on this issue to strengthen the validity of the results of the present study. Second, due to a lack of clinical trials and incomparable experimental data, we could not perform a meta-analysis. Third, based on the risk of bias evaluation, all experimental research contained significant sources of bias. Variations in units of Tau dosage (e.g., mg/kg/day, %, mM) among reviewed studies can also be considered as a fourth limitation. Since clinical research is frequently justified based on findings from animal research, this systematic review demonstrated the importance of developing high-quality randomized controlled trials to prevent the possibility of bias in future studies. The strength of the current study is to systematically review the related research about Tau in SLE. In addition, there were no limitations for time and language.

In conclusion, the present systematic review shows that Tau can play a role in SLE by attenuating inflammatory, oxidative stress, and apoptosis parameters.

The current systematic review merely describes available studies on the efficacy of Tau administration in SLE, outlines potential mechanisms, and recommends the need for additional controlled clinical trials to confirm these results, ascertain the optimal dose and assess safety and long-term efficacy.
